name: Pure
summary: Windows 11-inspired: Widgets, Start with your apps, and the tray float as three modules along the bottom, and nothing else is on screen.
description: The JERONIX desktop: three floating modules along the bottom. On the left, live updates (music, timers, downloads) that open the widgets; in the center, Start, search, Task View and your apps; on the right, Quick Settings, notifications and the clock. The Super key opens Start. The modules step aside under maximized windows, and GNOME's top bar and desktop icons are hidden. All standard GNOME keyboard shortcuts keep working.

settings.reason: Original JERONIX icons; anything JERONIX does not draw falls back to Adwaita.
Neutral, quiet system sounds.
Older (GTK 3) applications use a neutral dark theme with a blue accent.
A neutral, highly legible interface typeface.
Documents use the same neutral typeface.
JERONIX's primary look is dark; the light variant stays fully supported.
Blue is the JERONIX accent: buttons, switches and selections in every app.
A neutral monospace typeface for the terminal and code.
The neutral pointer.
The overview is Pure's workspace switcher, so it stays one gesture away.
The clock is the main persistent text in the panel; the weekday makes it useful at a glance.
Every window has minimize, maximize and close buttons on the right, where people coming from Windows expect them.
Super is the key: JERONIX turns it into the Start key (super-key-start-menu).
Workspaces appear and disappear as needed, so there is nothing to configure.
Secondary monitors stay put while workspaces switch, the GNOME default.
JERONIX light wallpaper.
JERONIX dark wallpaper.
Fill the screen without distortion.
Graphite shows while the wallpaper loads.
Lock screen matches the desktop.
The JERONIX name sits beside its symbol.
Fewer persistent elements; the overview shows workspaces.
A quiet top bar: menu, clock and status only.
The JERONIX menu replaces Activities.
The taskbar runs along the bottom edge.
Always visible, as on Windows 11: maximized and snapped windows fit above the taskbar, never under it.
Compact Windows 11 proportions.
Running applications appear after favorites.
Window previews on hover.
Three expandable modules: widgets on the left, Start and apps in the center, Control Center and notifications on the right.
Start, search and apps centered, as in Windows 11.
Quick Settings and the clock with notifications live in the taskbar tray.
One bar: GNOME's top bar is hidden while the taskbar carries the tray.
Task View opens the windows and workspaces overview.
The JERONIX Start button opens Start: pinned apps, recommendations, power.
Search finds apps, files and settings from the taskbar.
The Super key opens Start, as the Windows key does.
Task View shows windows and workspaces only; apps live in Start.
The left module shows what is going on (music, timers, downloads) and opens the widgets.

limitations: Window snapping is left to the system: GNOME's edge tiling, or Ubuntu's Tiling Assistant where it is installed (it turns GNOME's off while it runs).
The stock dock and desktop icons are switched off through disabled-extensions, never uninstalled; restoring the snapshot switches them back on.
Panel item order and the overview's own layout are GNOME's.
